title: Cell division pattern is the result, not the cause, of the form of the growing mass

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Cell division pattern is the result, not the cause, of the form of the growing mass

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The form of a growing organism regulates the form and number of the cells that compose it: the cell network is the result, not the cause, of the overall configuration, which is caused by whatever processes make growth faster in one direction than another.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The complex cell-network is not the cause but the result of the general configuration, which latter has its essential cause in whatsoever physical and chemical processes have led to a varying velocity of growth in one direction as compared with another.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter VIII, “The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)”; topic “Growth form determines cell division”. Scope: growing multicellular plant and animal structures

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch08-17: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.48

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The proposed variables are measurable, but 'overall configuration' and its causal priority require interpretation. Existing developmental imaging can test selected tissues, not the broad scope, and feedback between cell behavior and tissue form is a major confound.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use time-resolved tissue imaging to compare changes in organ-scale anisotropic growth with cell division orientation and topology. Competing causal models should predict whether tissue geometry precedes and explains cell-network organization or vice versa.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The claim spans plants and animals but data are concentrated in model systems.

Causal direction is difficult to establish from observational imaging.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.5
data existence: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.35
discriminating power: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Direction of causation can be turned into a comparison of strain and division, but only after choosing what counts as a decisive perturbation. Suitable movies exist for Arabidopsis, Drosophila and a few other systems, scattered across imaging archives rather than as one growth-versus-division table. That sample can test the relation in those organs and cannot cover the stated scope of plants and animals, and analysis means harmonizing datasets before any causal contrast is credible.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From time-lapse of growing organs, compare the growth-rate anisotropy field with the orientation and timing of division planes, and with organ shape after divisions are reoriented or suppressed. The claim is supported if shape and division geometry are predicted by the growth field, and weakened if division orientation changes form while growth anisotropy stays fixed.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Open imaging covers a few model organs, not growing multicellular structures in general.

Growth and division are mechanically coupled, so a correlation does not by itself settle which is cause.
